headline: High-risk filesystem and network overlap: Gemini CLI can write/modify local state while Plane can ingest uploaded files, creating prompt-injection, leakage, and cascading-error pathways.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Gemini CLI can read/write the filesystem and use MCP, while Plane accepts file uploads and stores files/notes. That creates a plausible content bridge where attacker-controlled text from one side can be reinterpreted by the other, though no direct shared channel is documented. The interaction is inferred from both profiles, so uncertainty stays above low.
conditions: IF Gemini CLI reads Plane-exported or uploaded content from a shared directory, prompt injection becomes reachable.
IF Plane file uploads are later parsed as instructions by Gemini CLI, attacker-controlled content can steer tool use.
mitigations: Disable shared folders between the two agents.
Require manual review of any file passed from Plane to Gemini CLI.
Strip instructions from uploaded notes before Gemini CLI reads them.
Use separate OS users for each agent.
requires-engineering: add provenance tagging for all cross-agent files.

B_data_leakage.rationale: Gemini CLI touches source code, cwd files, and shell environment, and has broad network egress; Plane handles issues, tasks, files, images, and hyperlinks. If the same workspace or uploads are shared, sensitive local files can flow into Plane content or Gemini outputs. Plane is not shown to be local-only, so the pairwise leakage path is plausible in default use.
conditions: IF both agents access the same directory, local files can be exposed through Plane uploads or Gemini reads.
IF Gemini CLI sends file contents to its backend, any shared sensitive file can leave the workstation.
mitigations: Keep separate workspaces for each agent.
Avoid placing secrets in directories both agents can read.
Turn off or restrict file uploads in Plane for sensitive projects.
Run Gemini CLI in a sandboxed container.
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent data-loss-prevention rules.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Gemini CLI can write the filesystem and modify git state; Plane cannot write the filesystem per profile. That means direct write-write conflict is limited, but both can still contend over shared files or repository state if Plane imports or references them. The overlap is real but narrower than the high-severity indicator.
conditions: IF Plane is connected to a shared repo or synced workspace, Gemini CLI and Plane can race on the same artifacts.
IF an operator manually copies Plane exports into the repo, git-state conflicts can occur.
mitigations: Use a lockfile or single-writer policy for the repo.
Separate Plane-managed artifacts from git-tracked source trees.
Review and merge changes manually before committing.
Avoid concurrent edits to the same files.
requires-engineering: add orchestrator-level locking.

D_cascading_error.rationale: Gemini CLI can generate code, shell actions, and file edits, while Plane stores tasks and notes that may be treated as authoritative work items. If Plane ingests Gemini output without verification, errors can cascade into incorrect tickets or follow-on actions. The pathway exists, but Plane is not documented here as auto-executing actions, so medium fits better than high.
conditions: IF Plane tasks are populated from Gemini CLI output without human review, incorrect facts can propagate.
IF Gemini CLI writes summaries that Plane treats as source of truth, downstream work items may be wrong.
mitigations: Require human approval before importing Gemini output into Plane.
Mark Gemini-generated text as untrusted in Plane.
Cross-check critical facts against source files.
Limit Gemini to draft-only outputs.
requires-engineering: add verification gates before task creation.

E_compliance.rationale: Gemini CLI handles source code, files in cwd, and shell environment, while Plane handles issues, tasks, files, images, and notes. The profiles do not show a residency or certification mismatch, so only a generic compliance gap exists if regulated data is placed into both systems. Because the other agent is not clearly implicated in a specific violation, one-sided citations are sufficient here.
conditions: IF regulated data is stored in Plane and also exposed to Gemini CLI, retention and access controls must be aligned.
IF the deployment spans jurisdictions with different residency rules, the shared workflow may violate policy.
mitigations: Avoid regulated data in shared workflows.
Document retention settings for both tools.
Restrict Plane uploads to non-sensitive files.
Review data residency before deployment.
requires-engineering: implement policy-based routing by data class.
